idiom_name: operator conventions on members or extensions plus Comparable/compareValuesBy
implementation_notes: Kotlin maps a fixed operator set onto fixed function names (a + b calls a.plus(b), a < b calls a.compareTo(b) < 0), and such an operator function may be a member or an extension - the language's mixin mechanism, since one extension operator in scope supplies the syntax for every receiver of the family. Comparable<T> already declares compareTo with the operator modifier, so implementing it in a data class yields <, <=, >, >= for free, and compareValuesBy/compareBy generate the comparison body for a family; data classes additionally synthesise equals/hashCode/copy. Keep the operator as a member when it must not leak beyond the module: extension operators are resolved statically, are visible wherever the import is, and can never be overridden by a subclass.
pitfalls: Extensions resolve statically and a member with the same signature always wins, so an operator supplied as an extension is not virtual and can silently disagree with a member implementation in a subclass.

The operator modifier is inherited from Comparable.compareTo but required on any new operator name: omit it and the expression stops compiling with an 'operator not applicable' error at the call site.
operator syntax does not remove JVM costs or contracts: BigDecimal/unsigned arithmetic still boxes, and equals/compareTo consistency rules still govern sorted collections.
